title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 8: Who Will Discipline Supreme Court Justices?
keywords: Who Will Discipline Supreme Court Justices?
removed from office only via impeachment
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's August 22, 2010 Inquirer column answering readers who, amid the Malaya Lolas plagiarism complaint, asked whether it is even proper for Supreme Court justices to discipline their own ranks: 'if not they, who will?'

How a justice may be removed: only by impeachment, initiated 'exclusively' by the House for six constitutional grounds and tried by the Senate's 'sole' power -- with no justice ever successfully impeached (the closest being the 2003 Davide attempt, halted in Francisco v. House of Representatives by the one-year bar)

Why the Court disciplines its own for non-impeachable offenses (which carry lighter penalties than removal): because no law vests that power elsewhere -- illustrated by Bar Matter 979 (2000) and In Re Biraogo (2009, a P500,000 fine and indefinite suspension), now institutionalized in the Internal Rules' Ethics Committee

His defense (against readers reacting to his 'How the Supreme Court can help P-Noy' piece) that an independent Court's duty is to check presidential 'excesses and abuses,' not to 'ambush his programs' -- reversing executive acts only upon 'grave abuse of discretion,' which he defines
sub_topics: The readers' question: in reaction to his earlier column on the Malaya Lolas Organization's plagiarism complaint, readers asked whether it is 'awkward, if not legally baseless, for the justices to discipline their own' -- to which he replies, 'if not they, who will?'

Removal by impeachment only: the Constitution allows a justice to be 'removed from office' only by impeachment, initiated 'exclusively' by the House for six grounds -- culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust -- with the Senate holding the 'sole' power to try

The closest call: on Oct. 23, 2003, Reps. Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Felix Fuentebella tried to impeach CJ Davide; in Francisco v. House of Representatives (Nov. 10, 2003) the Court barred transmittal of the articles to the Senate under the rule that no impeachment may be 'initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year'

The gap: the six impeachable offenses do not include plagiarism, and the only penalty Congress can impose is removal -- no office is expressly granted power to penalize justices for lesser wrongs (suspension, fine, censure)

Self-discipline for non-impeachable offenses: absent any law vesting the power elsewhere, the Court assumed it -- for the first time in 100 years on March 22, 2000, censuring a member and forfeiting 50% of his bar-committee fees for failing to disclose a relationship to an examinee (Bar Matter 979, In Re: 1999 Bar Examinations)

In Re Biraogo (Feb. 24, 2009): a justice found 'liable for GRAVE MISCONDUCT for leaking a confidential internal document,' fined P500,000 from his retirement benefits, disqualified from government office, and later suspended indefinitely from law practice -- the largest administrative fine CJP could recall -- with the power now institutionalized via the Internal Rules' Ethics Committee

Co-independent and co-ordinate: answering readers who asked why the Court should 'help P-Noy,' he explains that an independent Court checks the President's 'excesses and abuses' but does not 'blur his vision and ambush his programs,' upholding executive acts under the presumption of good faith and reversing only upon 'grave abuse of discretion'

The grave-abuse standard defined: an act 'contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence,' or done 'whimsically, capriciously or arbitrarily out of malice, ill will or personal bias' -- abuse 'so patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty'

stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional baseline: establishing the narrow, exclusive route to removal before explaining what fills the gap

stances.claim: For non-impeachable offenses carrying lighter penalties, the Court rightly disciplines its own -- as in Bar Matter 979 (2000) and In Re Biraogo (2009, a record P500,000 fine and indefinite suspension) -- because no law vests that power in any other body, and it has now institutionalized this through the Internal Rules' Ethics Committee.
stances.rhetorical_move: gap-filling justification: deriving the Court's self-discipline power from the absence of any alternative and its own precedents

stances.claim: An independent Court's duty is to check the President's 'excesses and abuses,' not to 'blur his vision and ambush his programs' -- so it upholds executive acts under the presumption of good faith and reverses only upon 'grave abuse of discretion,' a standard he defines precisely.

notable_anecdotes: 'If not they, who will?': CJP frames the column around readers' unease -- is it not 'awkward, if not legally baseless, for the justices to discipline their own?' -- and turns the question back on them.

The 2003 Davide attempt: he recalls how Reps. Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Felix Fuentebella tried to impeach CJ Davide, only for Francisco v. House to bar the articles under the one-year rule because an earlier complaint had already been filed.

The record P500,000 fine: he cites In Re Biraogo, where a sitting justice was found liable for grave misconduct for leaking a confidential document, fined P500,000 from his retirement pay, disqualified from office, and later suspended from law practice -- 'the largest fine ever imposed... for any administrative offense.'
Answering the 'help P-Noy' critics: he revisits the pushback to his Aug. 1, 2010 piece, explaining that checking abuses is different from sabotaging a President's lawful programs.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's August 22, 2010 Inquirer column, answers readers who -- reacting to his earlier piece on the Malaya Lolas Organization's plagiarism complaint -- asked whether it is 'awkward, if not legally baseless, for the justices to discipline their own. If not they, who will?' He begins with removal: the Constitution permits a justice to be 'removed from office' only by impeachment, initiated 'exclusively' by the House for six grounds (culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust) and tried by the Senate's 'sole' power. No justice has ever been successfully impeached; the closest was the Oct. 23, 2003 attempt by Reps. Teodoro and Fuentebella against CJ Davide, which Francisco v. House of Representatives halted under the rule barring more than one impeachment 'within a period of one year.' Since those six offenses exclude plagiarism, and the only penalty Congress may impose is removal, no body is expressly empowered to mete lighter penalties -- so the Court itself assumed the task, censuring a member for the first time in 100 years in Bar Matter 979 (2000) and, in In Re Biraogo (2009), finding a justice liable for grave misconduct for leaking a confidential document, fining him a record P500,000 from his retirement benefits and later suspending him from law practice -- a power now institutionalized in the Internal Rules' Ethics Committee. Finally, answering readers who bristled at his 'How the Supreme Court can help P-Noy' column, he distinguishes checking from sabotage: an independent Court must check the President's 'excesses and abuses,' not 'blur his vision and ambush his programs,' upholding executive acts under the presumption of good faith and reversing only upon 'grave abuse of discretion' -- an act 'contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence' or done 'whimsically, capriciously or arbitrarily,' so 'patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty.'
